findings.title: CreditManager _lzReceive payload parsing mismatch causes message decode failure
findings.description: In sendCredits(), the payload is encoded as `abi.encode(MSG_SEND_CREDIT, amount)` which produces a 64-byte ABI-encoded payload where MSG_SEND_CREDIT occupies a full 32-byte slot (padded bytes1). However, in _lzReceive(), the code reads `bytes1(payload[0])` and then does `abi.decode(payload[1:], (uint256))`. This creates a mismatch: sendCredits encodes with abi.encode (32-byte aligned slots) but the receiver on the CreditManager side expects a tightly-packed 1-byte prefix followed by abi.decode of the rest. If a remote chain sends a MSG_REDUCE_CREDIT using the same abi.encode pattern, the decode at `payload[1:]` will fail or return corrupted data because the offset is wrong (should be payload[32:] for abi.encode). This is a critical cross-chain message parsing bug that could cause fund accounting errors or permanent message failures.
findings.suggestion: Standardize the encoding/decoding pattern. Either use abi.encodePacked for the message type prefix followed by abi.encode for the data (and decode with payload[1:]), or use abi.encode for everything (and decode with payload[32:]). The sendCredits function uses abi.encode which pads bytes1 to 32 bytes, so the receiver should use `(bytes1 msgType, uint256 amount) = abi.decode(payload, (bytes1, uint256))` for consistency.

findings.title: CrossChainAssetController _lzReceive payload parsing mismatch with abi.encode format
findings.description: The _lzReceive function reads `bytes1(_payload[0])` to get the message type. However, the RemoteAssetAdapter sends messages using `abi.encodePacked(MSG_WITHDRAW_CONFIRM, amount)` (line 203 of RemoteAssetAdapter.sol). With abi.encodePacked, the bytes1 type is 1 byte, NOT 32 bytes. But then the code does `abi.decode(_payload, (bytes1, uint256))` which expects a 64-byte ABI-encoded payload with 32-byte-aligned slots. Since RemoteAssetAdapter uses encodePacked (producing 33 bytes: 1 byte type + 32 bytes uint256), the abi.decode will fail because the payload size is wrong for standard ABI decoding. This causes withdrawal confirmations and yield reports to silently fail, potentially leading to permanent fund accounting desynchronization between Hub and remote chains.
findings.suggestion: Align encoding/decoding across Hub and satellite. Either both sides use abi.encodePacked for the message type followed by abi.encode for the data parameters, or both use full abi.encode. The receiver should decode accordingly. Recommended approach: use abi.encodePacked(msgType) + abi.encode(params) on the sender, and bytes1(payload[0]) + abi.decode(payload[1:], ...) on the receiver.

findings.title: RemoteAssetAdapter silently drops cross-chain confirmation when gas is insufficient
findings.description: When the RemoteAssetAdapter handles a withdrawal, it attempts to send a confirmation back to Hub. However, if the contract has insufficient native balance for the LayerZero fee, the confirmation is silently dropped -- no error, no event, no revert. The Hub's CrossChainAssetController already optimistically decremented deployedAssets/totalDeployed when it sent the withdrawal command. Without the confirmation, there is no way to reconcile state if the remote-side withdrawal actually succeeded but the confirmation failed. This creates permanent accounting divergence between Hub and remote chain with no visibility or recovery mechanism. The same issue exists in _sendYieldReport (line 233).
findings.suggestion: Either: (1) Revert the entire _lzReceive if confirmation cannot be sent, so the LayerZero message can be retried later, or (2) Queue the failed confirmation in storage and provide a retry function that an operator can call once the contract is funded, or (3) At minimum, emit an event when the confirmation is dropped so operators have visibility.

findings.title: PPTOFTAdapter uses approve instead of safeApprove/safeIncreaseAllowance with potential race condition
findings.description: The _handleRedemption function calls approve() on the inner token to approve the redemptionManager for the share amount. However, this approval is set just before calling _requestRedemption, and there is a logical issue: if innerToken is a token that requires approval to be set to 0 before changing (like USDT), consecutive redemptions could fail. More critically, the function first calls approve and then safeTransfer in _requestRedemption (line 333), which is contradictory -- if the code approves the redemptionManager but then transfers directly, the approval is wasted. If the intent was for the redemptionManager to pull the tokens, the safeTransfer in _requestRedemption breaks that flow. This double-handling creates confusion about the actual fund flow and could lead to tokens being stuck.
findings.suggestion: Clarify the intended flow: if _requestRedemption transfers tokens directly, remove the approve call. If the redemptionManager is supposed to pull tokens, remove the safeTransfer and call the redemptionManager's function instead. The current code both approves AND transfers, which is incorrect -- only one mechanism should be used.

findings.title: CrossChainAssetController optimistic accounting creates unrecoverable state on remote failure
findings.description: The withdrawFromRemote function optimistically decrements all deployment tracking before the cross-chain message is confirmed. If the remote chain fails to process the withdrawal (e.g., insufficient protocol balance, paused adapter, gas issues), the Hub's accounting will show reduced deployment while funds are still deployed on the remote chain. The MSG_WITHDRAW_CONFIRM message from the remote is informational only (just emits an event) and does not restore accounting on failure. There is no mechanism to reconcile or roll back the optimistic update. For a system handling real funds, this creates a permanent divergence between tracked and actual deployed assets.
findings.suggestion: Implement a two-phase accounting pattern: (1) Mark the withdrawal as 'pending' without changing deployedAssets, (2) Only decrement deployedAssets when MSG_WITHDRAW_CONFIRM is received, (3) Add a timeout/cancel mechanism for pending withdrawals that never get confirmed. Alternatively, add an admin function to manually reconcile accounting if a remote operation fails.

findings.title: LiquidityPool removeLiquidity has no access control allowing anyone to drain pool funds
findings.description: The removeLiquidity function has no access control -- any address can call it and withdraw any amount up to the pool balance. There is no tracking of who deposited liquidity, so any caller can drain the entire pool including user deposits and credit-backed liquidity. This is a critical vulnerability because the pool holds actual user funds for instant withdrawals. The addLiquidity function similarly lets anyone add, but the removal without LP tracking means the first caller can steal all funds.
findings.suggestion: Implement LP token tracking (mint LP tokens on addLiquidity, burn on removeLiquidity) or restrict removeLiquidity to onlyOwner. At minimum, track deposits per address and only allow withdrawal up to the amount each address deposited.

findings.title: PPTSatellite deposit route through addLiquidity is unauthorized and will revert
findings.description: The deposit function in PPTSatellite calls liquidityPool.addLiquidity(assets) after approving. However, addLiquidity uses safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, ...) where msg.sender will be the PPTSatellite contract. The PPTSatellite already transferred assets from the user to itself (line 180), then approves the LiquidityPool and calls addLiquidity. This flow works IF the PPTSatellite has approved the LiquidityPool AND the LiquidityPool pulls from PPTSatellite (which it does via safeTransferFrom(msg.sender)). However, the architectural concern is that user deposits are routed into the liquidity pool and become withdrawable by anyone via the unprotected removeLiquidity (see RC-006). This means user deposit funds can be stolen.
findings.suggestion: Either: (1) Keep deposit assets in the PPTSatellite contract rather than routing to the LiquidityPool, or (2) Fix the LiquidityPool to properly track LP positions and restrict withdrawals. The current architecture conflates user deposits with instant withdrawal liquidity in an unsafe way.

findings.title: PPTOFT _lzReceive missing peer validation allows unauthorized minting
findings.description: The _lzReceive in PPTOFT does not verify the source chain or sender. While LayerZero's OApp base class validates peers at the endpoint level, the PPTOFT does not check that the message comes from the Hub (hubEid) specifically. The PPTOFTAdapter on Hub chain does validate peers (line 215-218), but PPTOFT on the satellite side does not. If a peer is set for any chain (not just the Hub), messages from that chain could mint arbitrary PPT tokens. The _credit function mints tokens without any additional validation.
findings.suggestion: Add explicit validation that `_origin.srcEid == hubEid` or that the origin is a specifically trusted peer. Although OApp's peer mechanism provides some protection, defense-in-depth for a mint operation on a fund-handling token is essential.

findings.title: LayerZero options encoding is incorrect -- missing required header bytes
findings.description: The LayerZero V2 executor options format requires a specific header before the option type. The correct format per LayerZero V2 documentation is: [OPTION_TYPE_WORKER_ID (uint8 = 1)][OPTION_LENGTH (uint16)][OPTION_TYPE (uint8 = 1 for lzReceive)][GAS (uint128)][VALUE (uint128)]. The current implementation starts directly with uint16(3) which does not match the documented LayerZero V2 options encoding. This will cause the LayerZero endpoint to reject or misinterpret the options, potentially causing all cross-chain messages to fail or execute with incorrect gas limits. This pattern is duplicated across all contracts (CreditManager, CrossChainAssetController, PPTOFT, PPTOFTAdapter, PPTSatellite, RemoteAssetAdapter, LzOptionsLib).
findings.suggestion: Use the official LayerZero OptionsBuilder library from @layerzerolabs/oapp-evm/contracts/oapp/libs/OptionsBuilder.sol. Example: `OptionsBuilder.newOptions().addExecutorLzReceiveOption(gasLimit, 0)`. This ensures correct encoding with proper headers and worker IDs. If you must encode manually, follow the exact binary format from the LayerZero V2 source code.

findings.title: CreditManager rebalance fee distribution can leave cross-chain messages unfunded
findings.description: The rebalance function splits msg.value equally across chains for LZ fees. However, different destination chains may have vastly different LayerZero fees. If chain A needs 0.01 ETH but chain B needs 0.001 ETH, splitting equally could underfund chain A's message, causing _lzSend to revert and the entire rebalance transaction to fail. Additionally, chains where credit is being reduced (newCredit < oldCredit) do not need cross-chain messages, but they still consume a fee slot in the equal division, wasting funds and potentially underfunding chains that do need messages.
findings.suggestion: Use _quote() to calculate the exact fee needed for each chain that requires a cross-chain message (only chains with increased credit). Sum those fees, validate msg.value covers the total, and allocate the correct fee per chain. Skip fee allocation for chains that only need local credit reduction.

findings.title: PPTSatellite _lzReceive missing reentrancy guard on mint operation
findings.description: The _lzReceive handler in PPTSatellite processes MSG_MINT_SHARES by calling pptOft.mint(receiver, shares). This function lacks the nonReentrant modifier. While typical ERC20 mints are not reentrant (no external calls to untrusted code), if PPTOFT has transfer hooks or if the receiver is a contract with receive/fallback functions that could trigger reentrant calls, the lack of reentrancy protection is a risk. Other contracts like CrossChainAssetController and RemoteAssetAdapter correctly apply nonReentrant to their _lzReceive implementations.
findings.suggestion: Add the nonReentrant modifier to _lzReceive in PPTSatellite, consistent with the pattern used in CrossChainAssetController and RemoteAssetAdapter.

findings.title: RemoteAssetAdapter _handleDeploy does not actually transfer or deploy assets
findings.description: The _handleDeploy function only updates accounting variables but never actually transfers tokens to the DeFi protocol or calls the protocol's deposit function. While comments say 'simplified', this means the Hub thinks assets are deployed to Aave/Compound but they are just sitting idle in the adapter (or not even there if assets were never bridged). Similarly, _handleWithdraw only updates accounting without actually pulling funds from the protocol. _calculateYield always returns 0. This is effectively dead/placeholder code that gives a false sense of functionality. In a fund-management system, this creates a complete disconnect between tracked state and reality.
findings.suggestion: If this is intentionally a placeholder, add explicit NotImplementedError reverts or mark the contract as abstract. If this is meant to be production code, implement the actual protocol interactions using the protocol implementations stored in protocolImplementations mapping. At minimum, the contract should transfer assets to/from protocol addresses.

findings.title: Duplicated LzOptions encoding across 6 contracts ignores existing LzOptionsLib
findings.description: A shared LzOptionsLib library exists but is not used by any contract. Instead, every contract (CreditManager, CrossChainAssetController, PPTOFT, PPTOFTAdapter, PPTSatellite, RemoteAssetAdapter) has its own private _buildOptions / _buildDefaultOptions / _buildLzReceiveOptions function with identical implementation. This violates DRY principle and makes the LzOptionsLib an orphan module with no callers. If the encoding format needs to be fixed (see RC-009), it must be fixed in 6+ places instead of one.
findings.suggestion: Replace all private _buildOptions variants with calls to LzOptionsLib.buildLzReceiveOptions(). This centralizes the encoding logic and makes future fixes or LayerZero version upgrades a single-point change.

findings.title: LayerZeroErrors library defined but never used by any contract
findings.description: The LayerZeroErrors library defines shared error types but every contract defines its own duplicate error types locally. For example, UnknownMessageType, ZeroAddress, InvalidAmount, ChainNotSupported are all redefined in CreditManager, CrossChainAssetController, PPTSatellite, RemoteAssetAdapter, LiquidityPool, etc. The library is an orphan -- it exists but is imported by zero contracts.
findings.suggestion: Either use the shared LayerZeroErrors library across all contracts to maintain consistency and reduce bytecode size, or remove it if per-contract errors are the intentional pattern. Currently it is dead code.

findings.title: PPTOFTAdapter _requestRedemption uses keccak256-based pseudo-random request ID
findings.description: The _requestRedemption function generates a requestId using keccak256 of block.timestamp, owner, and shares. This ID is not guaranteed to be unique (same block, same owner, same shares = same ID) and is predictable. For a redemption system handling real funds, request IDs should be sequential or use a nonce to guarantee uniqueness. Collisions could cause redemption tracking issues.
findings.suggestion: Use a sequential counter (uint256 private _nextRequestId) for generating unique request IDs, or integrate with the actual RedemptionManager contract which should provide its own unique IDs.
